utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Yesterday the examination-in-chief was concluded. So therefore, Mr. Crosland, you would expect cross-examination would start right away. Nevertheless, the Chamber would have one or two questions for you, and -- but before putting those questions to you I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. And you also have now seen that the Bench is now complete again, there are all three of us there. Mr. Crosland, my question needs perhaps a -- some introduction. Yesterday - and perhaps for the parties, would you please focus on page 2936, 2954, and 3018. Mr. Crosland, yesterday you used the word "technically controlling" an area. Then you were invited to explain what you meant by that, and you did so referring to a situation where a road would be blocked by 20 or 30 fighters with relatively light weapons. Then later on you were again using the terms "influence" or "controlling the area," and you said: "So saying that the KLA had control has got to be tempered with the fact that they were initially probably the goldfish in the bowl but very rapidly the Serbs became the goldfish in the bowl with the local population," that is where you used again -- you were referring to control, influence. And then finally when you were discussing the Dukadjin area you said: "It doesn't mean to say that the KLA owned the whole area, but it was more of a KLA influence in that area but it needs -- I mean, I think it would need further explanation." Well, we see that at several moments you used the word "control" or "technical control" and "influence." And since you said, specifically talking about the Dukadjin area, that it would need further explanation to the Court, the Chamber would like to receive that further explanation. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I make sure that we're all speaking about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When the witness was referring to technical control, he was referring to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the whole --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- to the fact that certain roads were the subject of roadblocks, and one of the areas of cross-examination I wanted to pursue with him is what the implications of that were for the territory in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When he was talking about 50, 60 per cent, three or four roads that was -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's one aspect of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The question and answer that Your Honour is referring to at the end of the day is very specifically related to a map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- on which he has drawn a red-lined area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so for the witness to answer any questions about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He'll refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- he will need to have the map in front of him. In fact, it was one of the areas I was going to go to quite early on in cross-examination. I'm perfectly happy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether he needs the map or not, but at least he indicated it would need further explanation, if you would need the map for that further explanation, Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, it would probably help the Court because the people may not be familiar with some of the names of the villages and towns and I think it would probably be easier to demonstrate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could that map be --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I then indicate how I was proposing to start with cross-examination so that Your Honour sees the materials that are available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We have two files of materials available for cross-examination of Colonel Crosland. The first is a slimmer green bundle which you have on your bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the second is a much larger blue file. It's hoped that the blue file won't be necessary. It's the green file I'll be concentrating on. Behind tab 1 in the green file is the map that Colonel Crosland was referring to, and I've also arranged for Colonel Crosland and Your Honours to have a clean copy of map 6 from the bundle which we were trying unsuccessfully yesterday to discern on the screen. But the map that the witness was giving evidence about at the end of yesterday afternoon is behind tab 1 of the bundle. So might the witness be given the bundles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- and then the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Crosland, is really focused on the portion of your evidence where you said this may need further explanation. I only referred to the earlier portions of your testimony because similar words were used there, and some of them explained, sometimes not explained in full detail. So could you please then answer my specific question on what you would like to add as far as explanation is concerned. And could the map be shown on the -- let me just see whether -- I haven't got the -- that's the marked map with the area in the middle. Madam Registrar. Mr. Crosland, the map will be showed on your screen soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: While waiting, maybe I could ask an additional question to ask -- in order to have a complete understanding of the picture, Mr. Crosland, could we get back to that notion of the technical control. I just was asking myself, and I think it's very relevant to the Bench, what in -- as this is in military language, I understand these are technical terms, what would be the contrasting concept as opposed to technical control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, good afternoon. I apologise for confusing the Court yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try and unconfuse people. The whole business of trying to understand the situation in Kosovo obviously required constant monitoring of both sides of the potential conflict. The conflict started, as I said yesterday, after the Donji Prekaz incident, in my opinion, and continued throughout 1998 and into 1999, as we're well aware. In order to better understand the situation, it was partly my own initiative to go out and seek out the Kosovo Liberation Army in order to try and give a more balanced account of what was going on. As I said yesterday, Your Honours, this is an operational area, and it is an extraordinary feat that the Vojska Jugoslavije and the MUP actually allowed foreigners, like myself, to work inside an operational area, that was both very demanding and very dangerous for everyone concerned. When you also look at the fact that in the early days of 1998, the Kosovo Liberation Army was probably very fragile, quite disjointed in its separate groups, and in most of the areas in country that is not advantageous to, if we may call them, guerilla fighters because the Serbs had heavy weapons with long ranges and could seek out targets that could not possibly reach them by return fire. So in order to try and build a more in-depth and accurate assessment of the intelligence picture, it meant attempting to get to visit and to be trusted, if one is quite blunt, by the KLA, that we could represent them more accurately. Initially this came through, as I said yesterday, Your Honours, a political contact in Pristina, no doubt heightened by the fact that Mr. Holbrooke and various other international community people, Lord Ashdown came into the area or into Albania and Mr. Holbrooke into Junik, and therefore the international community started to get an interest in what was going on in then a sovereign state of Serbia. So those are some of the thoughts I would lay before you that one was trying to get a balanced picture and to present that picture in various diplomatic telegrams, situation reports, and direct phone calls back to Belgrade and to London and to other headquarters, as the situation itself unfold. I think yesterday we got - forgive me for saying - slightly bogged down, but I did try to explain that there are inevitably gaps in the reporting system, because as I believe when the ICTY approached the Ministry of Defence in London in 1999 to start this current Tribunal, they handed over various documents, some of which are redacted, which is not a word I was familiar with, but that's the black line across various documents. And not all documents, as I understand it, were passed across. Now, I don't know the actual list, so hence there are gaps in the knowledge, and this is causing some confusion as to what went -- what happened when and where. In my own particular case, I have made numerous statements which in this cut-and-paste world I'm afraid there have been some mistakes. I'm not attempting to confuse or mislead the Court, but we are in a cut-and-paste world and I think that has added to some of the confusion where dates have been transmitted erroneous and not been picked up, for which I can only apologise. I hope that gives you an opening answer to one of your questions, Your Honour. The technical control, if I may go on, after the Donje Prekaz incidents happened throughout the province of Kosovo with the KLA attacking and the MUP and the Serbian forces responding, but by about I suppose April/May the Serbs, from my point of view, more or less admitted that they did not control three of the four roads. They were blocked as I indicated yesterday at various places coming from the north at Rakos outside of Rudnik, at Likosane in the middle road from Pec to Pristina, and outside Stimlje south of Urosevac, leaving the Strpce road, the mountain road, as the only road open. That situation lasted, if I can remember quite rightly, until the Serbs mounted a major summer -- late summer/autumn offensive when they then cleared these three routes. These routes were blocked by fallen trees, use of old vehicles, and what I would call very minor defensive positions. I drove through I think all of them on several occasions, and there may have been 20 or 30 fighters, if I leave it at that, in these areas. No doubt, they may have been able to call on some more, but if you look at the strength, potential strength that the Serb security forces could employ against them, these were -- they were just technically in control, they were allowed to be in control. Now, why this happened, I have not -- never received any information from the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, is -- would your answer be in any way different because you give a general picture and you express one as a surprise that the Serbs allowed this to happen. Yesterday there was this specific reference to this map where you said KLA was in the middle, was in red.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There you specifically said that -- where you said KLA did not own the whole area but it was more of a KLA influence, but that -- that would need further explanation. Is that a similar explanation that you just gave, that is, that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This -- Your Honour, this area we're looking at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the Dukadjin area in essence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the interior part, I don't think anyone managed to get across that in the nearly two and a half years I was down there. It was not a well-known area. There was reports of mining on the various tracks, and therefore one of the principles, as probably the most senior and most experienced person, was that if you don't need to go down there, then don't go down there. The Serbs likewise took up a position that they could, if you like, contain the fighters within this area by dominating the roads. I don't agree with the strategy, but that was the way they did it. So the area remained -- the Serbian security forces would go off the road a short way, make a raid, re-arrange a few houses rather badly, and then withdraw back out because they didn't feel safe in the area. Now, that was their way of dealing with localised incidents that happened in and around these major proceeds from Pec to Klina down to Djakovica and back up to Pec. So the roads provided the access, and not often -- I mean, one of the major incidents was going -- the Serbs -- we were asked to go with the Serbs to visit this supposed massacre site at Glodjane -- beyond Glodjane on the concrete water area. Now, I don't think many of them went further than, say, 5 or 6 kilometres off the road because they were going into a territory that they really were not that familiar with. So that is why I've said that that area, in my opinion, and it is only my opinion, was basically a KLA area and the Serbs would stay on the outside and attempt to dominate and influence areas by shelling into the area or long-range indirect fire by tanks or by armoured personnel carriers or anti-aircraft vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what you meant that the KLA did not own the whole of the area, but they were more or less forced to stay in there and now and again at the edges and the marginal -- margins they were pushed back. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They -- as I said yesterday, Your Honour, the situation was extremely fluid throughout because no one side really held ground, apart from the garrison towns and things like that, which was obviously the preserve of the Serbian security forces, but we must realise that, as I said yesterday, the population was I think 5 or 6:1 in the Albanian favour. So even in the towns the Serbs were outnumbered in the majority of cases, until of course we had the movement of Albanian villagers, disbanded, displaced personnel, which is another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers, Mr. Crosland. Mr. Emmerson, are you ready to cross-examine the witness, Mr. Crosland?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I am ready to cross-examine but may I raise first of all the question of timing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I will do my level best to make as much progress and even aim to complete today, if possible. But I think I have indicated in advance that this is a witness with whom I'm likely to need more time than is usual, and some of the questions that Your Honour have just asked and that the witness has just answered raise potentially fairly fundamental questions about this indictment and the Prosecution's case theory, and I need, therefore, to have the opportunity to develop with Colonel Crosland some contemporary documentation that may assist in refreshing his memory about what the position was in fact on the ground during the period that we are concerned with in this indictment. So I simply want to lay down the mark at this stage that it is possible that we may ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, the Chamber of course encourages very much if you could finish cross-examination today, but in view of how the parties use their time until now, where it was clearly announced that you would need more time for the cross-examination of Mr. Crosland, that even if you would not manage, we'll find a solution so that the Defence -- and that of course is true for all Defence counsel -- is not deprived of its rights to cross-examine the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before I start asking some general questions about Serb deployment which is where I want to begin, can I just pick up one or two of the questions that the Judges just asked you and then precisely -- there were really two sets of questions. One is the meaning of "technical control" deriving from the interruption of the main arterial roads running from east to west, and the second is the rather more specific question of incursions into the area marked in red on that map.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So I think there may have been some linguistic issue about the word "technically" that arose, because my impression from, certainly Judge Hoepfel's questions, is that he was under the impression that the expression "technical control," was a form of -- a term of military art. Can I ask you this. I want to just put to you a question and answer that I think deals with this specific point that you were asked and gave in the Limaj trial and see if this encapsulates the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is for those wanting to follow in the transcript 2009, line 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Mansfield, he said to you: "Effectively, therefore, what you were saying in your own assessment was that the apparent efficacy of the KLA and control has been or was exaggerated in the minds of others, when in fact on the ground it was fairly thin. I'm putting it in colloquial language. Is that fair?" To which you replied: "I wouldn't necessarily disagree with that, no." And then he goes on to ask you this: "I give an example. You described the three roads and how they were blocked and so on. I think at one point you say in one of your narratives of this that just because they were able to interrupt the passage of transport on those roads by no means meant that they controlled the areas of territory between the three roads, although people assumed that?" And you replied: "Yes, this is, as I said yesterday, sir, where I disagreed when people said they controlled 35 or 65 per cent. This was what was being put forward but I would caveat it with the fact that as I've said all the way along, there was a lack of proper use of military force by the Serbian authorities." Now, is that a fair summary of the position that you're describing when you use the expression "technical control"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. We have to put a date/time into this. If you're talking about the early period between March, April, May, June, possibly July, then this was the way that some people would refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have tried to do is to say, in my expression, technically, yes, they blocked the roads, but this was not, in my opinion as an experienced officer, a credible force at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Again, just so that we're clear, you used the expression earlier on just a moment ago in answer to Judge Hoepfel's question, you used the expression "just technically they controlled the roads." Now, have I understood it correctly. Are you effectively saying -- are you effectively saying it was technical control but not necessarily actual de facto control of the territory in between those roads?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in trying to answer your question as honestly as possible, from a military point of view I didn't consider these vehicle check-points as any threat to a determined Serbian assault, if they had been prepared to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can't answer that question why or et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Precisely, sir. I'm going to come back to the other area, the specific area that you've marked on the map in quite some considerable detail during the course of this afternoon, but I want to start then in my cross-examination with you by asking you some questions about the deployment of the Serb military and security forces. And just to indicate the overall structure. I want to deal with those questions first and the questions about the modus operandi of the Serbian operation during 1998 and 1999. One or two questions about your understanding of command/control responsibility on the Serbian side; in other words, who was in and who was not in the command loop in the area that we're concerned with.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I then want to move on to a selection of DipTels, sitreps, and documentation emanating from the VJ and other organisations, chronologically, so that we can try to build up a picture of what the position was on the ground. And then by way of one or two other questions I want to come to the canal towards the end. But can I start then by asking you some questions about military deployment. For this purpose I wonder if you would take the green file and turn to tab 6. Now, tab 6 should be -- behind tab 6 it should be a DipTel dated the 26th of March, 1998, which is largely concerned with security matters and which records your assessments of the Serbian security forces which, as at the end of March, were deployed and balanced, you say in paragraph 2, to mount a joint strike in the Decani-Gjakove and Drenica-Lausa-Vodnik areas. And I want, if I may, to go through those forces with you just to ensure that I've got a proper understanding of them. But before I do can I ask you first of all about the VJ itself, the VJ's deployment itself and four particular personalities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't wish to interrupt but just for the identification purposes of this document so that it's not lost, I think Mr. Emmerson is referring to Exhibit P927 from the Limaj trial. We've got them all listed in the index we handed up yesterday. It would very much assist not losing these if my learned colleague referred to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not going to be in a position to do that. I collected them together with other documents in this bundle which -- all of which will be in due course exhibited. I'm happy to provide a list and there's one available to the registry during the course of the day, but I don't, if I may say so, want to spend time trying to cross-refer it to the exhibits as we're going along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with the exhibits and what is what exactly at a later state. We now are focusing on what is R0428505.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think, if I may say so, it will become clear by reference to the dates of the documents as well but which will be on the transcript, so there will be no difficulty with that and the tab numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: First of all can I begin by asking you about VJ deployment. You answered some questions about that yesterday. Can you just remind us first of all, by this time, by the end of March, total numbers, please, first of all, of VJ deployment in Kosovo as a whole in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as I said yesterday, the major unit, the formation unit in Kosovo is 52 Pristina Corps, based in Pristina. And as the forward or formation of 3rd Army based in Nis. They had based in Kosovo at that time between 10 and 13, 14.000 men, stationed in three or four major brigade areas in Prizren, Urosevac, Pristina, and Gnjilane, if I remember correctly. So that was the formation that we were dealing with on the initial deployment, and one could arguably say that those were, you know, the legal troops. I guess I shouldn't use the word "legal," but those were the troops stationed in Kosovo as a forward base.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'll come to look at some of the other forces in a moment or two. Personalities for a moment. The overall head Chief of General Staff of the VJ at this time was General Perisic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he was based in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was not regularly or routinely deployed in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would come down from time to time and particularly more so as the situation deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Began to deteriorate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Then the Chief of military security on the General Staff was General Dimitrijevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was chief of counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Chief of counter-intelligence. And so really two -- the most and one of the most senior officers in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: A little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, moving down to Kosovo level and to 52 Pristina Corps, General Pavkovic was in overall command of 52 Pristina Corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That was the position as of March --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of -- it then changed. I think he then became -- he took over command of the 3rd Army and then ultimately Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I referred to him a moment ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- also for the witness. You're speaking the same language. Would you please make a small pause after you have put the question, and once you've answered the question first a small pause and then the next question; otherwise, the transcribers can't follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise to Your Honours and to the interpreters and to the transcribers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think I referred a moment ago to General Pavkovic. Was he, therefore, in command of 52 Pristina Corps throughout the period from March to October 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And General Ojdanic, at what point does he begin to feature and in what capacity inside Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Ojdanic was the Chief of Staff of the Vojska Jugoslavije, the VJ, based in Belgrade, and he produced a brief to the Belgrade Attache Association I think, if I recall, the 27th or 28th of August to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- inform people about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I understand, please, the command relationship between General Perisic and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Ojdanic was working directly to General Perisic as part of the higher Vojska Jugoslavije staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now may I move down one tier and to the VJ deployment in western Kosovo and the area with which we are concerned, as represented on that map. At the time there were, were there not, two principal VJ brigades, the -- and if I get my military terminology wrong, do please correct me. The 125th, commanded by Colonel Dragan Zivanovic, based I think in Peje --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In Pec, I'm sorry. And the 549th under the command of Colonel Bozidar Delic, as he was, based in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the border-line between those two, was it ever clear to you exactly where that border-line ran between the areas of responsibility of the 549th and the 125th?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that physically, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We've been looking at this road running from Peje down to Gjakove --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- and as far as you can remember, would there -- would the boundary between their areas of responsibility bisect that road or is that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would guesstimate that the boundary would be somewhere possibly around Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think, if I may say so, that may prove to be a pretty close guesstimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, it's my lack of knowledge of the English language, but is a guesstimate, is that an --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: A guesstimate is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- estimate with some guesses in it?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly. And that's with a degree of guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's an estimate that acknowledges the uncertainty of its own position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in fact, it's a word I'm going to come back to later on if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, if I can, with that background, understand what you believed to be the constitutional function of the VJ in guarding the borders and the limits of its constitutional function?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So on the -- one of the previous occasions, I think someone went into this in great detail and told me that I was wrong in my assessment; however, what I was told when I first joined as the Defence Attache in Belgrade from the foreign liaison service was that the Vojska Jugoslavije had primacy on and around the border areas, international borders, of the former Yugoslavia, from 500 metres to approximately 2 kilometres. Therefore, most of the interior was under the primacy of the MUP, Ministry of the Interior, police and their relevant formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, whatever the true constitutional position, your understanding of that position had a direct impact, did it not, on how you went about conducting your observations, because you were constantly looking, were you not, to see whether there was evidence of VJ forces becoming involved in military action directed specifically at the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, sir, in that as the conflict grew in intensity, it became clear that elements of the Vojska Jugoslavije and in particular, equipment had been painted blue as opposed to green, and this was mainly armoured personnel carriers and anti-aircraft BOV-3, as we call it technically, anti-aircraft triple-barrelled devices, which were then attached to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that was something that you kept a careful eye on, because your understanding was that the VJ themselves ought not to be being engaged in those types of operations. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite, sir. I mean, I -- it's very impolite of me to tell another country how to conduct its military operations. What I was concerned, though, was that the amount of force being used was disproportionate to the -- the guerilla fighters that were then against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm going to come, obviously, to the disproportionality of the force that was used. But just on this one point, you told us a moment ago that vehicles which had been green were being painted blue. Can we ensure that everyone understands the significance of that. Are you telling us that VJ vehicles and heavy weaponry which by being painted green would be clearly identified with the VJ, was being repainted blue to make it appear as though it were regular police equipment being used by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And amongst that equipment, you mentioned the BOV-3. That is one of a number of heavy anti-aircraft items of weaponry. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, may I ask one clarifying question. If you say it was painted blue where it was green before, do you intend to say that this equipment was handled by the same crews as before or would, apart from the colour, also the crew change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- Your Honour, I cannot confirm whether the crews were changed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You understand what I mean by --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the crew, that is, whether it would be a police crew -- or a MUP crew rather than a VJ crew and not whether the same persons were involved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand you entirely, Your Honour. I cannot confirm that the crews were changed or were not changed. The point I have made on several occasions was that this extremely heavy weaponry and equipment was -- had been repainted in blue in order to try and confuse people that this was normal, standard equipment for the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it was finally used by the MUP, whether standard or not, you can't answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think it may be that, as I say, as we progress through some of these documents, it will become quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Those items of heavy weaponry we were just discussing, the BOV-3 is one example, they are built for anti-aircraft operations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What were they used for in the Serbian campaign in Kosovo, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were used as heavy close support in firing into villages or houses along the roads in support of ongoing Serbian security operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So they were being used on, effectively, personnel and property rather than on airborne targets?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As far as you know, in principle, is that consistent with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, sir, I made a comment that I believe it is not consistent; although I myself came under aircraft -- anti-aircraft fire in the Falklands, so perhaps it was pay-back time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the reason, in your view, for the lack of consistency is the complete disproportionality of using such heavy weaponry in an indiscriminate fashion against civilians and civilian targets. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, and I think it's been well-documented in a lot of my reports that one continued to see devastation on a major scale throughout the spring, summer, and into the autumn and beyond of 1998, and obviously into 1999 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If we can just zoom down to western Kosovo for a moment. Did you see those heavy anti-aircraft weapons painted blue moving around in the region of western Kosovo that we're concerned with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did you see them frequently?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, were they used to shell the villages that we see on these maps?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was quite clear that they -- and, I would suggest, the tanks, the heavy tanks had been used as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I come now finally to this DipTel and to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, perhaps one -- the question was: "Were they used to shell the villages that we see on these maps." Could you please seek clarification whether all of the villages or whether some of the villages or --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to, if I may, in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm reasonably confident by the end of this cross-examination that Your Honours won't be looking for more detail from me but less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You say - and I'm using the word "you," because it's reporting your analysis in this 26th of March DipTel behind tab 6, for the record - that your assessment was that the Serbian security forces were balanced to mount a joint strike in two areas, one of which, of course, is the area we are concerned with, the Decani-Djakovica area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you describe in the following paragraph, paragraph 3, three levels of forces. Now, we're not here speaking about VJ, are we?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we're not, sir. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We're speaking about combined police, special police, and RDB, state security forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So just reminding yourself of what's in the DipTel for a moment, I think -- first of all, 3(A), the outer ring, you describe A, B, and C as an outer ring, an inner cordon, and an assault force. An outer ring, you say, capable of deploying 8 to 10.000 MUP for urban deployment, crowd control, assisted by imported thugs. Smart cars seen from Ivangrad and various other places which I think are in Montenegro. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority are, yes. Novi Pazar is not and Mitrovica obviously, Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Obviously, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll come back to the thugs in a moment or two. The 10 -- 8 to 10.000, is that a reference to regular MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a reference to regular MUP in -- deployed in and around the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Kosovo as a whole?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then an inner cordon of 5 to 700 PJP holding an inner ring of VCPs, that's vehicle check-points, around the operational area supported by 10 to 15 APCs, armoured personnel carriers, with heavy cannon. Now, first of all, PJP, could you explain to us what the PJP was.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the PJP is a special police unit which, I suppose, are like heavily armed riot control police, we don't have an equivalent in England, who were there for carrying out what I would call the basic infantry tasks, leaving the MUP to hold the outer cordon and provide external security, whilst the -- the initial assault would go in -- the PJP would assist in the assault. They were well-armed, much more aggressive, and came, as I said, from several areas outside of Kosovo because we could see that from the vehicle registration plates of their particular vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, pausing there for a minute. When you say "outer ring and inner cordon and assault force," are those, if I can use the analogy of concentric circles, are they concentric circles at the centre of which would be a particular attack? Is that what you are conveying?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What -- the modus operandi was that the area would be controlled by the outer cordon, so they would keep people out.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that would be conducted by the ordinary MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: By -- normally the ordinary MUP. Internal to that you would then have a light infantry force available to back up a very specific assault force of the SAJ and other people, who were the specialist assault troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, pause there for a moment. So we've got the outer ring of MUP controlling the area. We then have what you've described as infantry. I think in one of the other cases where you've given evidence you used the expression "grunt infantry, barely policemen." What does that mean, "grunt policemen"? Does it have a special connotation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is exactly what it says. I mean, they are not -- they are dressed in the particular uniform that the PJP wore, but their actions were more like a very heavily trained riot, anti-riot section of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And they would be armed with automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then spearheading the assault itself would be either or both of forces derived from the SAJ or the JSO. Is that what you're conveying in this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, before we turn to the SAJ and the JSO, I just wanted to ask you one or two questions further about the PJP. You've given there an estimate of the numbers. Did you ever come across a group affiliated with the PJP or working alongside them in the same uniforms known as the Mundza?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't come across that particular name, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you haven't heard of them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever see PJP officers in uniform with a lightning bolt on their arm?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't recall that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Now if I can turn to the specialist assault forces, the SAJ and the JSO. First of all, the SAJ, what were they? How would you describe them and what sort of arms and uniforms did they have?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said here, they were the anti-terrorist unit, probably about 200-strong, and their equivalent was the JSO, who were also another anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So these were two anti-terrorist units, armed and trained, and pausing for a moment on the SAJ, again, were you aware of an SAJ unit or a unit affiliated to the SAJ known as the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- no, not particularly, sir. They were several names bandied about in Kosovo, the Eagles and the Black Eagles and the Black Hand, and until one could actually attempt to try and verify what was correct and what was the name of the day, we kept it as simple as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I put the question bluntly to you. Was it your assessment or were you aware that within the uniformed PJP and within the uniformed SAJ, there were personnel who had been former irregular paramilitaries operating under the Serbian forces in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, there were -- as I said, there were rumours about all sorts of connections. But as you, I think, will appreciate, it would be extremely difficult to get someone to admit that they had been connected with any nefarious activity in further parts of the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Although, as I think we see later on in some of your sitreps, there may be some evidence for those connections. Let me then move to the JSO. Appearance-wise and equipment-wise, would there be a distinction between the JSO and the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have given detailed descriptions of this in previous testimony so --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You can take it very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were much better armed, they were much better equipped, they looked much more professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And they were not within the VJ or the MUP structure, but reported directly to the RDB, the Serbian State Security. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I think you knew two or came across two of the JSO's leaders inside Kosovo, one of them Frenki Simatovic on one occasion, and the other one a man whose nickname was Legija?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legija.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Legija. First of all, did you have an opportunity to speak to Frenki Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met. We were staying in the same hotel in Pec, and apart from "good afternoon," I don't think there was any further conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You know, obviously, that Frenki Simatovic has been indicted in respect of war crimes in Croatia and Bosnia. Were you aware that the JSO itself was a successor organization to the Red Berets in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd heard -- yes, and they wore a red beret, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And Legija, you met, I think, near Lapusnik sometime in the middle of the summer. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And his correct name I think you probably know by now, if you didn't then, is Milorad Lukovic or Milorad Ulemek. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's not a name you've heard?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard the name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he was known to have been a member of Arkan's Tigers in Bosnia, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'd heard indications of that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he was the ultimate leader of the JSO in Kosovo, as he told you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we met on the Lapusnik crossroads above Malisevo, he informed me that he was the leader of this particular assault group that also had Vojska Jugoslavije tanks involved in it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you were witnessing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you often insisted that the Prosecution would seek further clarification of vague rumours or "I heard this" --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to do that right now, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But as I do, you personally witnessed Legija preparing to mount a joint operation between the JSO and the VJ. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he personally spoke to you and told you that he was in charge of that operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in my report, I think he was a bit surprised that we had just come from his objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But can you confirm that he told you that he was in command of that operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he lead me to believe, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did he lead you to believe he was in charge of the JSO or the VJ and the JSO that was stationed there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presumed that he was in charge of the entire operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And can I ask you this: Are you aware - and tell us if you're not - but are you aware that he has been convicted of murdering officials of the Serbian Renewal Movement and is currently serving a 40-year prison sentence in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So those were, if you like, the uniformed paramilitaries. Could you now tell us about the imported thugs that you're referring to there. Did you at times see groups of men who were not in uniform but who were in 4-by-4 vehicles and with Montenegrin and Macedonian and Belgrade number plates?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did indeed, sir, and I think -- I did indeed, sir, and I think that was in Pec, if I remember rightly, as one of the main places.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So I think on one occasion you followed them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because you wanted to know if these were irregular paramilitaries. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were attempting, as I said before, to find out as much detail, and I suppose because of my background I tended to be rather more inquisitive than some other people might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And when you followed them did you cross the border into Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I think if you're -- if the incident you're referring to, we went down into Rozaje, if that's the one, then that is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And when you got there did you see them corralling with large numbers of other men of similar appearance?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, if that's the same report you're referring to, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were there occasions when these men were seen with earpieces, communication earpieces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that there were, sir. I mean, one has to understand that the Balkans was in a state of unrest during this time, and many people were employed on "security duties."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: And therefore earpieces were standard fit. Whether they were connected to anything is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, standard fit for people who are connected in some form or another to the Serbian security apparatus?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a common piece of equipment used for communications, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just to be clear, though, you're looking at a group of men. That was the -- one of the factors that led you to conclude that these people were part of the Serbian security apparatus. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. These men were fit, well turned-out, smart, good vehicles and fairly purposeful so --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think in one report you said that your assessment was that elements of the RDB, that is the State Security Service, may well be involved with them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You've expressed the view in the past that you are confident that paramilitaries were engaged in western Kosovo in Pec and in Djakovica. Is it those men that you were referring to when you had made that assessment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think having seen these men in the Pec-Djakovica area, one would -- one could presume that they were potentially involved. It's -- it's a difficult question to put a definitive answer to because there were a lot of people wandering around dressed quite smartly but not in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You've also, I think, in one of your statements said this: "I am confident that Arkan's men were brought in from Montenegro." Again, was that a view you confidently held?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We attempted to find a base to the north of Mitrovica, which had been suggested to us that that was a paramilitary base. We were not particularly well received up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were you aware of an occasion when an ITN photographer was attacked for trying to take photographs of men matching these descriptions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have made a report, sir, to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think when you gave evidence in the Milutinovic case about this group of men, I'll just read to you a passage from your evidence. For those following, it's 9772, line 1. You said: "I think it's been made clear in the NATO report that these personnel had had experience in Bosnia, and therefore as part of the overall armoury of the Serbian security services, if you wish to call it that, these personnel would be used in operations as they had been done, had been used throughout the Bosnian war." Can I ask you, please, what was the NATO report that you were referring to there, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't specifically remember that report, sir. I would suggest it was probably a NATO or even a Ministry of Defence report on assessment from the Bosnian war which, obviously, one looked at in order to try and get a better understanding of what was going on within the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So when you said that as part of the Serbian security forces in Kosovo, and you said "those personnel would be used as they had been used throughout the Bosnian war." Can you explain, please, what you meant by that. How were they used in the Bosnian war?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were used within the Bosnian war as -- to provide an element of terror and fear into a civilian population. And sadly, this is all part of a -- mounting a counter-terrorist operation that was now underway within Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What would they do in Bosnia to put fear into the civilian population, what type --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think all their acts are well documented, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In a sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were shootings and killings that were obviously accredited to these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Random killings of civilians in order to terrify the population. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think both civilian and military were killed, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever see those men outside of Peje or Gjakove, in other words, on the roads between or only in the towns themselves?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were the odd vehicle driving around the area. It depended on the security situation. So I don't -- I think sometimes they were in -- probably in Pristina as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would these people operate clandestinely?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as much as you can operate clandestinely in a smart 4-by-4 in what is ultimately a rural area so --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I mean, for example, do you know whether -- let's just take the area you've marked on that map, do you know whether during the period from March to September any contingents of that group would have entered that area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be surprised if they didn't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You would be surprised if they didn't?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You'd expect this group of paramilitaries, whose function had been killing and causing terror in the civilian population, to find their way across territory like that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and unfortunately incidents draw people like flies to a jam pot.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You see, you may not know this, but before a trial begins the Prosecution and Defence are required to file a written statement of their case, which is called a pre-trial brief. And your map that you've marked is attached to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief as the basis for a suggestion that the area you've marked was an area of total exclusive KLA control into which Serb forces could not penetrate.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's, if I may say so, sir, a correct -- an accurate assessment of what I said. It was an area that was very difficult for the Serbs to penetrate, and you're also talking about, if I may remind you, about paramilitary and other clandestine forces who are not going to come to the British Defence Attache and tell them what they are going to do after dark or when he is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly, sir. And quite apart from the un-uniformed paramilitaries, I think in one of your reports you say - and we'll come to it in due course - you say -- you've cited the JSO in the area we're discussing -- I say western Kosovo along the road, I think it may have been on the western side of the road, but you've cited the JSO and you say, Worryingly, my Defence Attache has seen a contingent of the JSO. These troops are rarely seen. Now, I just wanted to be clear. Was it the position that the JSO, too, would keep a low profile?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite naturally. They -- their operations and their modus operandi is to do it as quietly and as carefully as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I mean, would you expect those anti-terrorist troops at least, if not the VJ, to be mounting clandestine operations in an area such as this, where they believed the KLA to be?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be very surprised if they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. So, I mean we -- just to be clear, we do need to understand your map as an area of influence of the KLA, but into which it is more than likely that anti-terrorist paramilitaries, whether in uniform or out of uniform, were making clandestine forays during the indictment period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be surprised if they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So when you told us a little earlier on that generally the MUP would only go in 5 or 6 kilometres, that that was referring to those troops which operate, if I may put it this way, above the radar screen that you could be aware of. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's more or less correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But even they penetrated this area regularly, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not I'm saying that. I'm saying is what I saw is what I reported --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I can't say that they went in or out 5 or 6 -- the area when I saw them going in, down to Rznic and Prilep was about a kilometre's in to the Radoniq canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We're going obviously to look at all that. But, in fact, you've recorded quite a number of instances in your reports where there have been engagements in Glodjane where people have been shot in Glodjane or near Lake Radoniq, right in the area we're discussing in conflicts between the VJ and the MUP on the one hand and the KLA on the other. That's basically right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the Vojska Jugoslavije and the MUP had bases in and around this area which became targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Can we just turn over the page in this report. I just wanted to ask you about the second sentence in the paragraph under tactics. "Positions very obviously designed to dominate by terror rather than tactically sighted indicating probably thinking about a short, sharp strike." And then just a little further down, PJP and MUP vehicle movements you say again: "A show of force similar to early times in Bosnia." What was it you were trying to convey by those entries?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, if I remember correctly, that whilst they had quite obviously more than sufficient strength to carry out operations in these areas, their tactics were not particularly credible in that it was just a whole mass of men on a vehicle which does actually provide a terrorist with a very easy target.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said "dominating by" -- I'm sorry, that's not the word -- yes, "dominate by terror"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if villagers and civilian population sees a heavily armed military force moving into an area, not unnaturally they will be frightened as to what is going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you now - and this is something of a generalisation, I think, but rather than asking you about specific engagement which I'll turn to, I just want to ask you about an overall assessment of the modus operandi as the conflict wore on in the year. I want to just -- and I apologise for keeping -- continuing putting to you words that you've used in other contexts, but sometimes it's the shortest and simplest way of inviting you to comment. In one of your witness statements you say this, and I quote: "I myself saw between 200 and 300 villages burnt throughout 1998 and into 1999. Crops were just wantonly burned. Businesses of all sorts, for example, petrol stations and shops were looted and within towns like Decani, Pec, and Djakovica, the Albanian areas were completely burnt-out. This included damage to mosques. Some villages had been looted and burnt at least on three occasions, with the civilian population leaving and then returning once they thought it was relatively safe to come back." You've made other statements in other words saying much the same thing at various times. Before you tell us about the civilian population leaving and coming back, can you just summarize for the Judges how those operations were conducted and with which forces doing what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initial statement about the 2 to 300 villages, Your Honour, is made in several reports throughout 1998 and 1999 as a way of trying to convince the international community and the various other foreign powers who were interested that the behaviour of the Serbian security forces was not acceptable to the situation that was in Kosovo itself. The words of ethnic cleansing were not -- I was not allowed to use because ethnic cleansing has a legal connotation which I'm sure the Court is far more well aware of than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to use. I'm just asking you to describe what you saw.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw, as set out in that paragraph, exactly what Mr. Emmerson has read it. I don't think I can say any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Who was -- which troops were involved and what were their roles in the destruction and the burning and looting of the groups we've described, VJ, SAJ, PJP, JSO, paramilitaries -- who was doing what when you were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of these formations were involved in destroying and destruction of both villages, businesses, crops, houses, and mosques, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you see properties being looted?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And who would be doing the looting, men in uniform or men out of uniform?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones that I saw were men in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And what sort of things were they taking out of people's houses?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Rakovina, on the road up from Djakovica, I saw a PJP with a wheelbarrow with a television in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then when they'd looted the houses, was it after that that they would burn them down?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not an ongoing purpose -- sorry it was an ongoing project of most operations. And when challenging the Vojska Jugoslavije rumour, I'm not accredited to the MUP --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I mentioned this fact on several occasions in 1998 to General Ojdanic, in particular, and other people, that the behaviour of the Serbian security forces was only driving the Albanian population into the hands of the Kosovo Liberation Army, whether they wanted to go or not. And the behaviour of many troops, myself and my colleagues on several occasions, were actually fired at by Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And again, just to get the favour of this absolutely clear. Did you see animals shot and crops and animal feed stacks being burnt and destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What did you understand to be the purpose of killing the animals and destroying the feed for the winter?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've just mentioned the word "winter." And during -- as the 1998 proceeded when more and more people, Albanians primarily, but also Serbs as well, were being driven from their homesteads, then obviously the problem would be how these -- these people would survive the winter when the homesteads had been burnt, their crops had been burnt, and their animals had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I mean, was it your assessment that this was being done to make it impossible for the Albanian population to return to these villages because they --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly wouldn't encourage them to stay where they were, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Their livelihoods were finished?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their livelihoods were incredibly badly damaged, but to their great personal courage and determination, a lot would try and return to their homesteads and continue their life as best as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think you know, don't you, because you've said so in one of your reports, that when these attacks would happen the KLA would very often move in and try and put up a defence against them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes, but bearing in mind the disproportionate force that was -- was or could be used against, I think most of the time the Serbs would achieve their objective and then withdraw to let the Albanians pick up the bits and pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is it right that your ambassador, based on what you told him, saw Mr. Milosevic and conveyed the British government's view that what was going on amounted to crimes against humanity?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that's correct. It's in one of the DipTels, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think in the Limaj trial itself, it was put to you, and you agreed, that what you yourself had witnessed by the Serbian security force was a widespread and systematic attack on the civilian Albanian population. And you agreed with that. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that statement, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, just finally on this area, we went through a list of names in the VJ earlier on. Were you raising your concerns with VJ officers, senior VJ officers, throughout the summer about your belief that the VJ were providing fire cover for these type of destructive operations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's documented, sir, that I produced that -- General Ojdanic's briefing details of these activities --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That was in August I think, was it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: End of August.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I had other meetings earlier in the year, with both General Perisic, with my ambassador on some occasions, and with General Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you were told -- putting it bluntly, you were told lies by some of the VJ officers who you spoke to, the senior officers, about VJ involvement. It was bluntly denied to you, on a number of occasions, that the VJ had any role in any of this when you yourself had seen it with your own eyes and had video evidence of it. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time when you were having conversations with General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic, in which it became clear to you that those two very senior officers in the VJ were being cut out of the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have made a comment of that in one report, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They told you, in effect, that there was a direct line of command between Pavkovic and Milosevic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that they were being kept out of the loop because they disapproved of what had happened in Kosovo and weren't prepared to go along with the use of the VJ for these type of operations. Is that what they told you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, I think, Ojdanic on one occasion, at the end of the summer, agreed with you that the operations across the summer had been grossly disproportionate, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, just so that we're clear, the VJ forces who were involved in these engagements were the forces commanded by Bozidar Delic and Dragan Zivanovic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular area, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Did you know that they were witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would you regard their evidence about control on the ground and their involvement as credible, based on what you were told by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would hope that the two brigade commanders, as they were then, would understand the command and control system on the ground, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, apart from asking you to slow down a bit, I would like to give you 25 minutes to think that over.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break, 25 minutes. We'll resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, I just want to pick up on an answer you gave just before we broke where you said that you hoped that the two brigade commanders would understand the command and control system. Can I ask you to comment on this. At what level of command would the authorisation have been given within the VJ for VJ forces to conduct the shelling cover for these destructive operations that you have described?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I think we have to back-track, if we may, a little bit. During the process in 1998 the opinion we formed was that there must have been a coordination centre in, probably Pristina which is where the corps headquarters, the army formation headquarters was, along with the major MUP headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this would be a perfectly sensible procedure to go through. Now, for a long -- a long time, the Serbian security forces denied that there was such a control centre. We managed to find out by intelligence means that there was a control centre there. So that is where I presume the orders were being issued from corps headquarters down to the specific units that were either under the control of 52 Corps headquarters or units that were then drafted in to this operational area. And therefore, the commander of the operational area, in this case General Pavkovic, would have been the operational commander, and his Chief of Staff would have probably written the operational order for him. And that would then be sent down to the subsequent and junior formation commanders, the two brigade commanders that we have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you look very briefly -- and I don't want to go through the contents of it in any detail, but could you look briefly behind tab 38 in that bundle, where we have a document headed: "Meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija."
